Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Rob Oliver explains why embedded software moats can survive cheaper coding while seats, pricing and direct AI competition pressure valuations. Eisman accepts that some incumbents will adapt but avoids the group until growth estimates become clearer, suggesting at least a year. Later ServiceNow and Tyler growth supports operating resilience without settling that timing call. The stock-compensation critique is economically sound, but public software companies do report GAAP alongside adjusted results.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

### 017. Adding stock compensation back to adjusted earnings makes recurring labor costs disappear from the emphasized profit metric; in his example $50 economic profit becomes $75 adjusted profit.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

The conditional relationship follows from the explicit assumptions; it does not establish that those assumptions hold in observed markets.

## Framework and tools

- Separate software creation cost from enterprise deployment and maintenance.
- Analyze seats, prices, usage and renewal cohorts separately.
- Distinguish survival from valuation and shareholder returns.
- Include recurring share compensation in economic cost.
- Use proprietary data and workflow depth to differentiate vendors.
- Wait for evidence that can discriminate among competing narratives.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Forward sales and FCF multiples.
- GAAP and adjusted earnings reconciliation.
- Renewal and net-revenue-retention cohorts.
- Software buyout leverage and entry valuations.
- Tyler municipal workflows and AI adoption.

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman interviews Rob Oliver. Oliver supplies differentiated company analysis; Eisman states his own avoidance position, pricing concern and accounting critique.
- Full transcript read in two contiguous parts including closing takeaway.
- Recording described as day before Good Friday, implying April 2 2026; publication is April 13.
- Guest is Rob Oliver; closing caption mangles his name.
- One Citrix description conflates remote access with backup; treated as incidental terminology rather than a separate material thesis.
- No public price-series audit was completed, so later company results are not treated as proof of stock-return success.
